Senators sent a sweeping infrastructure package to the House on Tuesday, handing Majority Leader Dana Whitfield a bipartisan win after a spring and summer of stop-and-start talks over how federal road money should be split.

Seventy-one senators backed the five-year plan. Most Democrats voted yes, joined by Republicans from largely rural states whose governors had lobbied hard for bridge funding. Twenty-seven senators opposed it, a mix of fiscal hawks worried about the price tag and a handful of progressives who argued the package leans too heavily on new highway lanes at the expense of trains and buses.

The real fight may come next. House Speaker Paul Renner told reporters last week that his members would insist on rewriting the formula that decides how much each state receives, and farm-district lawmakers have complained that big cities come out ahead under the version the Senate approved.

Inside the administration, officials were relieved. Secretary Lena Ortiz, who runs the Transportation Department, warned in a statement that states could see payments for ongoing projects slow down if the House lets the current program lapse at the end of the month.

The measure's biggest line items are bridge repair and a pot of grants for freight routes serving ports. Critics note that it relies on borrowing rather than a higher gas tax, which has not risen since 1993 and brings in less every year.

Whitfield, speaking to reporters after the vote, said she expected the House to pass something similar before the deadline. Renner's office declined to give a timeline.
